summary: Provides suggestions for system administrators and implementers of FTP servers to decrease the security problems associated with FTP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The old file-sharing method has some weak spots. This is a list of tips to make it harder for bad guys to take advantage.

questions: how to secure an ftp server
what is an ftp bounce attack
why does ftp send passwords in clear text
subtitle: A short checklist of ways FTP servers can be abused, and how server authors and administrators can blunt each one.

tldr.problem: The FTP specification lets a client tell a server to send a file to a third machine, and allows unlimited password attempts. Attackers can use both to hide their tracks and to guess passwords.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests refusing data connections to low port numbers, limiting password attempts, delaying replies to bad passwords, hiding which usernames exist, and using random data ports.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance, not a standard. The authors say the suggestions reduce FTP's security problems without removing functionality.

today: RFC 2577 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is advice for implementers, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why FTP Needs Security Advice
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol (RFC 959) lets a client open a control connection and have one FTP server transfer a file directly to another server. This proxy FTP saves network traffic, which is handy when the client sits behind a slow link such as a modem.

The same feature allows a bounce attack, and FTP servers can also be used to guess passwords by brute force. RFC 2577 gives advice to FTP server implementers and system administrators. It does not cover FTP combined with strong security protocols such as IP Security.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP can ask one computer to send a file to another. That is useful, but a bad person can misuse it, so the authors wrote down ways to stop that.

sections.title: The Bounce Attack
sections.content:
The attacker sends an FTP PORT command that names the address and port number of the machine and service to be attacked. The attacker then tells the FTP server to send a file to that service. The file can hold commands for the target service, such as SMTP or NNTP.

Because the FTP server makes the connection, the real attacker is hard to track down, and network-address-based access restrictions can be circumvented. The RFC's example: upload a file of SMTP commands, point the server at a third machine's SMTP port with PORT, then order the transfer. That can forge mail without a direct connection.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like asking a friendly delivery person to hand a rude note to someone else, so nobody can tell the note came from you.

sections.title: Defending Against the Bounce Attack
sections.content:
FTP puts no limit on the TCP port used for a data connection, while ports 0 to 1023 are reserved for well known services. The RFC therefore suggests that servers not open data connections to TCP ports below 1024. A PORT command naming such a port should get reply 504, "Command not implemented for that parameter". Servers on ports above 1023 stay exposed.

Other precautions: protect uploaded files with proper file protections, since the attack usually needs an upload followed by a download, and take similar care if data connections use a protocol other than TCP. Disabling PORT is also an option, because most transfers can use PASV alone. The cost is losing proxy FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is a rule: do not deliver to the busiest, most important doors. If you never need to deliver for others, you can turn the service off.

sections.title: Protecting Passwords and Usernames
sections.content:
To limit brute force guessing, servers should close the control connection after a small number of attempts (3 to 5), and must send reply 421 first. The RFC also suggests a 5 second delay before replying to an invalid PASS command. An intruder can open several parallel control connections, but limiting connections or refusing a suspicious site opens the door to denial of service against valid users.

Standard FTP sends passwords in clear text, so clients and servers should use authentication mechanisms that resist eavesdropping, such as those in RFC 2228. To stop attackers learning valid usernames, a server should always answer USER with 331 and reject the username and password pair later, instead of answering 530 for unknown names.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone keeps trying keys on your lock, make them stop after a few tries and wait a bit. Also, never tell them which names are real.

sections.title: Address Checks and Port Stealing
sections.content:
A server that limits access by network address should check the remote address on both the control connection and the data connection. Otherwise a trusted host could open the control connection while a different host receives the data. Clients should likewise verify the address of whoever connects to a port they opened in listen mode. Address checks still allow spoof attacks, so secure authentication should be used when possible.

Port stealing works because many operating systems hand out dynamic ports in increasing order. An attacker makes a legitimate transfer, guesses the next port, and connects to it. That can block another client, steal a file, or insert a forged file. The mitigation is to use random local port numbers for data connections.
sections.plainLanguage: If tickets are handed out in order, a sneaky person can guess the next number and cut in line. Handing out random numbers makes that guessing hard.

sections.title: Privacy and Software Bugs
sections.content:
Standard FTP sends all data and control information, including passwords, unencrypted. The RFC says a strong encryption scheme should be used whenever possible, and points to RFC 2228 for one.

Many documented FTP problems come from poor implementation rather than protocol design. The RFC names three features abused in the past: anonymous FTP that lets users read all files or create files, the optional SITE EXEC command that runs arbitrary commands on the server, and software installed with debugging features enabled. Implementers are told to review the relevant CERT advisories before release.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain FTP talks out loud where anyone can listen, so secret talk should be put in a code. Some features, like letting visitors run commands, need extra careful handling.
